verdict.summary: GitHub OAuth apps are instantly self-serve with no manual review or verification required to deploy and allow outside users to connect.

evidence.note: GitHub does not have a formal verification queue for standard OAuth apps to function in production.

verification.note: You can create and register an OAuth app under your personal account or under any organization you have administrative access to.

evidence.note: Standard app creation and flow implementation takes minimal developer time.

wait_days.applies_to: None required for standard OAuth apps

evidence.note: No review queue exists for regular OAuth apps.

verification.note: OAuth apps can be created directly through settings without stating any required manual review or waiting time.

blockers.description: Marketplace listing requires an organization-owned app, minimum user thresholds (200 users), and publisher verification.
blockers.applies_when: You want to list your app on the GitHub Marketplace

evidence.note: Marketplace requirements specify minimum installation thresholds and organization ownership.

verification.note: To publish a paid app... your app must be owned by an organization that is a verified publisher... OAuth apps should have a minimum of 200 users.

prerequisites.item: A personal GitHub account to register the application.

evidence.note: Anyone with a personal account can create an OAuth app.

verification.note: You can create and register an OAuth app under your personal account...

steps.title: Choose Between OAuth App and GitHub App
steps.detail: Review whether your integration needs standard user-delegated scopes (OAuth App) or fine-grained repository permissions, short-lived tokens, and bot capabilities (GitHub App). Use OAuth apps primarily if you need enterprise-level resources.
steps.notes: GitHub strongly recommends GitHub Apps unless enterprise permissions are required.

evidence.note: Differences between GitHub Apps and OAuth apps documentation.

verification.note: If your app needs to access enterprise-level resources... you should use an OAuth app because a GitHub App cannot yet be given permissions against an enterprise.

steps.title: Navigate to Developer Settings
steps.detail: Log into GitHub and go to Settings > Developer settings > OAuth apps, then click New OAuth App.
steps.notes: Requires human login to the GitHub console.

evidence.note: Instructions for creating an OAuth app.

verification.note: In the upper-right corner... click Settings. In the left sidebar, click Developer settings. In the left sidebar, click OAuth apps. Click New OAuth App.

steps.title: Register the OAuth App and Configure Redirect URIs
steps.detail: Fill out the application name, homepage URL, description, and up to 10 callback URLs. Optionally enable Device Flow or expiring tokens.

evidence.note: Details fields required when creating an app.

verification.note: In Application name... In Homepage URL... In Authorization callback URL... up to 10 callback URLs... click Enable Device Flow...

steps.title: Retrieve and Secure Credentials
steps.detail: Save the generated client ID and securely store the client secret, noting that the secret is shown only once.
steps.notes: Client secret management is critical for backend token exchanges.

evidence.note: Getting client id and generating secret.

verification.note: Source 5 mentions client_secret and client ID but does not state that the secret is shown only once.

steps.title: Implement the Authorization Flow
steps.detail: Build the Web Application Flow or Device Flow pointing to https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize and exchanging codes at https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token, incorporating PKCE (S256).
steps.notes: Can be fully implemented in code by an AI agent.

evidence.note: Authorizing OAuth apps documentation.

verification.note: OAuth implementation supports standard authorization code grant type... code_challenge... S256

steps.title: Test with Your Own Account
steps.detail: Trigger the authorization flow using your own personal GitHub account to ensure scopes are requested correctly and tokens are successfully parsed and stored.
steps.notes: Verifies that redirect URIs and scopes match your implementation.

evidence.note: Testing requires manual account authorization.

verification.note: Source 5 does not mention testing with your own personal GitHub account to ensure scopes are requested correctly.

steps.title: Deploy for Outside Users
steps.detail: Release your application to production. Since standard OAuth apps have no review queue, outside users can connect immediately.
steps.notes: No provider approval is required for standard deployment.

evidence.note: Instant deployment availability.

verification.note: Standard OAuth apps are created immediately and self-serve via Developer Settings without a review queue.

evidence.note: Verified by test and documented.

pitfalls.description: Failing to validate user identity after every sign-in, as users can switch accounts during authorization.

evidence.note: Documented pitfall regarding account switching.

verification.note: Every time you receive an access token, you should use the token to revalidate the user's identity. A user can change which account they are signed into when you send them to authorize your app, and you risk mixing user data if you do not validate...

pitfalls.description: Assuming refresh tokens are always returned without checking if expiring tokens are enabled.

evidence.note: Token expiration behavior documented.

verification.note: ...your app should not assume that a refresh token is always returned.

pitfalls.description: Requesting broader scopes than necessary, such as using 'repo' when 'public_repo' or 'repo:status' would suffice.

evidence.note: Documented scope best practices.

verification.note: Source 6 lists available scopes and descriptions, but does not explicitly claim or warn against requesting broader scopes than necessary.
